I understand that the president wants to fill the court with who she believes is best before she leaves office, but I think that the court should reflect the will of the people. We have 13 circuit courts, and the people should pick a president who they believe should put in 13 justices that will represent the people”."}}, {"model": "campaign_trail.answer_feedback", "pk": 90202, "fields": {"answer": 90202, "candidate": 41421, "answer_feedback": "“I simply disagree with the president. By the time the final states get called, chills run down your spine. You can only stare at the television, speechless at what you are watching. How could this have happened? Did the country really disapprove of me this much? Decades of Democratic buildup gone, in one night, on your watch. This is your worst nightmare. The Decision Desk is in utter shock; Fox News is panning down on an ecstatic watch party in Miami. Looking out your window, all you can see are empty streets. People had just started to get out of their homes again following the pandemic, and suddenly, it all stopped in an instant. You can’t even begin to imagine the firestorm you’re having to wake up to in the morning. Party leaders turning their backs on you, Conservatives gloating about their victory, and Tim Kaine trying to save himself politically.

The chaos didn’t stop for a second in the following days. Each of Marco’s appointments got worse and worse with every announcement. He knows that Congress cannot stop him; his large victory gave him a filibuster-proof majority in the Senate. And you know, deep down, what will happen to the country because of it.

Looking forward, your post-presidency seems to be looking better than you’d had hoped. After four, unfortunately long, years in the White House, you’ll be joining your husband in retirement with the same title. That’s not to say you won’t be occupied, though; you still have a Presidential center to build, maybe a book to write, and causes that could be worth your time.

But for now, there is little time to think about that. Your Presidency may not have ended the way you expected, but given the circumstances, there is still time to save your legacy. By conducting a proper transfer of power, you’ll be able to remind the country of the professionalism and bi-partisanship you were able to show as President. Something you wished had been done four years ago.

{"min": 183, "max": 209, "html": "

Shortly after the polls closed, your watch party could tell it wasn’t going to be your night. The music died down before 10 o’clock, and people started to head home. You were shocked. How could they call the whole thing? Polls in the west coast hadn’t even been closed yet when the Decision Desk declared Marco the winner. The polls had shown that it was going to be an uphill battle for some time, but was it really this bad? Your advisors had told you the race was tightening. As Rubio’s jubilant watch party plays in the background, you look out your window. An empty party and street were left behind by the last of those at your watch party who had gone home. All you saw were people cleaning up the mess they had left, and your advisors trying to make sense of what they had just watched. You can hear some of them faintly talking outside of the room, but don’t bother to wonder what it is they’re talking about. You enjoy the moment of peace alone in the room, trying to forget whatever tomorrow will entail.

In the following days, the quiet, surprisingly, didn’t stop. Most of your advisors and staff had already prepared for the possibility of you moving out, and a lot had been going on behind the scenes without you. It seems that most of the people in your White House are simply looking to move on, and move past the time you were here. At least you hope not.

Looking forward, your post-presidency seems to be looking better than you’d had hoped. After four, unfortunately long, years in the White House, you’ll be joining your husband in retirement with the same title. That’s not to say you won’t be occupied, though; you still have a Presidential center to build, maybe a book to write, and causes that could be worth your time.

But for now, there is little time to think about that. Your Presidency may not have ended the way you expected, but given the circumstances, there is still time to save your legacy. By conducting a proper transfer of power, you’ll be able to remind the country of the professionalism and bi-partisanship you were able to show as President. Shortly after the first polls closed, you and your team were watching the returns at your watch party back in DC. Music was playing, the crowd was lively, and it reminded you of the fantastic atmosphere you had in New York four years ago. But slowly, as the night kept on, the map grew redder and redder, and your watch party grew quieter and quieter. The same people cheering and dancing just a few hours ago had left early to recuperate before a final call was made. You watched in awe as the Decision Desk finally called it for Marco Rubio. Was it really going to end like this? You looked out the window to see the few remaining from your watch party go back home. When you turned back, the screen panned in on a lively crowd at Rubio’s watch party in Miami. Part of you knew, deep down, that the outcome was going to be this. Despite how desperately you wanted to avoid it, you couldn’t ignore what the signs were showing. You can’t even imagine what tomorrow will entail, let alone the next few years, but that will be a problem for when you fall asleep. For now, you watch as the last of the returns come in.

The despair didn’t seem to stop in the following days. Your advisors are out of a job, Tim is figuring out what the future holds for him, and Bill is still shocked by your loss. You feel some of it too; the losses that have built up for your party over the past twelve years have given Marco a hefty majority in both Legislatures– at the peril of you and your predecessor's agendas.

Looking forward, your post-presidency seems to be looking better than you’d had hoped. After four, unfortunately long, years in the White House, you’ll be joining your husband in retirement with the same title. That’s not to say you won’t be occupied, though; you still have a Presidential center to build, maybe a book to write, and causes that could be worth your time.

But for now, there is little time to think about that. Your Presidency may not have gone and ended the way you expected, but given the circumstances, there is still time to save your legacy. By conducting a proper transfer of power, you’ll be able to remind the country of the professionalism and bi-partisanship you were able to show as President. No, no, no, this can’t be. Polls had been showing the race tightening within the final weeks, but you didn’t think that it would end up like this. You’re watching the Decision Desk in awe as neither you nor your opponent are able to make it over 270 electoral votes. The country is already in uproar. You can see people taking to the streets right outside your window; your advisors are speechless, your phone has stopped buzzing since Nevada was called, Rubio has already demanded recounts in various states, Trump is calling out election fraud– and people are beginning to believe he was right all along. You can’t begin to fathom the firestorm you will wake up to in the morning, or the protesting that is to come in the next few weeks.

The chaos didn’t stop for a second in the following days. You’ve been through dozens of meetings to analyze if there is even a chance for you to have a pathway in the House, or even Tim in the Senate. But you know it deep down: that is it. You and your predecessor's losses down ballot have come back to haunt you, and despite the small gains you made this year, it isn’t nearly enough to get you or your Vice President another four years.

Looking forward, your post-presidency seems to be looking better than you’d had hoped. After four, unfortunately long, years in the White House, you’ll be joining your husband in retirement with the same title. That’s not to say you won’t be occupied, though; you still have a Presidential center to build, maybe a book to write, and causes that could be worth your time.

But for now, there is little time to think about that. Your Presidency may not have gone the way you expected, but given the circumstances, there is still time to save your legacy. By conducting a proper transfer of power, you’ll be able to remind the country of the professionalism and bi-partisanship you were able to show as President. Something you wished had been done four years ago.

{"min": 270, "max": 295, "html": "

Shortly after the polls were closed, the signs weren’t looking good for you. The returns were mixed, and you weren’t hitting the same marks you had been hitting four years ago. As the night progressed, your watch party got dimmer– the music lowered, the chatter quieted, and people were hovering over their screens. And then, all of a sudden, something switched. Late into the night, it was finally called for you. The weight that had been over you for what felt like decades had gone away in an instant, and the party quickly restored itself to how it was four years ago. As you prepared your speech, you looked out your window to see a crowd of relieved and jubilant supporters of yours. But when you turned your head back, you caught a glimpse of the Decision Desk panning over Marco Rubio’s watch party. The crowd isn’t disappointed, but angry. Angry at what they believe was an election that was institutionally meant to go to you. You had just gotten off the phone, Marco. He conceded, so why is everyone concerned about the validity? As you get up to go give your speech, you want to enjoy this moment and your victory, but all you can think about is the response of Rubio’s supporters.

This anger only grew in the following days. Protesters swarmed through DC attacking your presidency and the election; the same people calling out election fraud four years ago are doing it again at an even louder level, and your approval has seen a downturn because of it. It’s all reminding you of four years ago, but something’s changed. You can’t decide if it was how close the election was, the change in your opponent, or if something had fundamentally changed within the country. As much as you hope the last part isn’t true, deep down, you know that the country isn’t the same from 10, or even 5, years ago.

Looking forward, the rest of your presidency isn’t looking too bright. The House and the Senate barely budged, and Republicans kept their majorities in both chambers. What you had hoped would be different from the last four years seems to be an exact replica. That’s not to say there isn’t a lot of work that you still need to do. Crucial conflicts abroad and a pandemic and its after-effects still need to be handled here at home. Play your cards right, and you could go down in the history books as one of the most consequential presidents of this century thus far.

But for now, you have to get the election legitimized first. Your first term may not have gone the way you expected it to, but you can break the cycle by ensuring that the country has their trust in you and to meet with Marco to ensure that the country can have faith in the electoral process. Something you wished to have done four years ago.

{"min": 296, "max": 307, "html": "

You’d given it your all during the final stretch of the campaign, and you were ready to relax. Early voting data had shown mixed signals for you, and you weren’t sure if you were going to see another four years come election night. When the first polls closed and people started to fill the room of your watch party, it made you forget about everything that had been going on– the constant campaigning, interviewing, attacks, and travel. As the night progressed, the party started optimistically, but cautiously. Soon after, though, the Decision Desk was able to declare you the winner. You had expected a long night, so to end this quickly was a shock to you, and most of the signs had expected it to take longer to call as well. Part of you knew, deep down, that it would end like this for you. All the long days and nights you had spent getting results had finally paid off. All there was left for you to do was step out into the rowdy crowd and give your speech, something you could only dream of doing just a couple of months ago.

This excitement didn’t last for long, and resentment toward you from the right grew in the following days. Conservative media figures and politicians spread claims of fraudulent voting methods that were discussed during the campaign. You had expected this to happen, but given Trump’s claims four years ago, you weren’t expecting people to actually go along with it this time.

Looking forward to the remainder of your presidency, it looks like much is going to be the same as the last four years. While you picked up several seats in the Senate and the House, none of the gains were able to get over the large Republican majorities and flip the chamber in your favor, but that’s not to say that there still isn’t more that can be, or should be, done. Crucial conflicts abroad and a pandemic and its after-effects still need to be handled here at home. Play your cards right, and you could go down in the history books as one of the most consequential presidents of this century thus far.

But for now, you have to get the election legitimized first. Your first term may not have gone the way you expected it to, but you can break the cycle by ensuring that the country has their trust in you and to meet with Marco to ensure that the country can have faith in the electoral process. Something you wished to have done four years ago.

The moment the first polls close, the nerves struck you. This wasn’t four years ago; polling had you in a dead heat, and the Republicans nominated a seasoned Senator to face you– not a 5-point lead going into election night and a billionaire who had never been in politics. The initial returns looked grim for you; the Northeast was looking to shift right and the same people who voted for you four years ago were skeptical about making the same decision. But once the 8 o’clock polls closed, you knew that these nerves weren’t going to last. A map scattered with blue quickly swept through as the night progressed and, somehow, you were outperforming how you did four years ago. As more and more states got called to you, the crowd outside your window got louder and louder. At last, as the Decision Desk declared you had won reelection, you walked over to your window to see how your watch party was doing. Your watch party was full of a sea of people watching in awe as the results showed a defiant win to secure you another four years. When you look back at the TV, as it pans over Marco’s watch party, the crowd looks deflated and angered. To enjoy the moment, you quickly turn off the returns and prepare to step out for your victory speech.

The excitement of this night was quickly challenged, though, and the shock of your victory wasn’t just among your own supporters; Republicans’ only explanation for your big win is election fraud. Because of this unease, your disapproval among Republicans has soared to an all-time high. You had expected this to happen, but given the margin of your victory, you weren’t expecting people to actually go along with it this time. Hopefully you can guide the country to avoid this response in the future, but deep down, you know this can only be solved by something far greater than your own actions.

Looking forward to the remainder of your presidency, it looks like much is going to be the same as the last four years. While you picked up a couple seats in the Senate and made the House more competitive overall, none of the gains were able to get over the large Republican majorities and flip the chamber in your favor, but that’s not to say that there still isn’t more that can be, or should be, done. Crucial conflicts abroad and a pandemic and its after-effects still need to be handled here at home. Play your cards right, and you could go down in the history books as one of the most consequential presidents of this century thus far.

For now, you have to get the election legitimized first. This should be a breeze given your win, maybe. Your first term may not have gone the way you expected it to, but you can break the cycle by ensuring that the country has their trust in you and to meet with Marco to ensure that the country can have faith in the electoral process. Something you wished to have done four years ago.

The moment the polls closed, you knew the night was going to be unforgettable. Before everyone had trickled into your watch party, people were already calling it for your reelection. As the polls closed on the west coast, a sea of blue had swept throughout the entire country. Something you couldn’t even fathom, not even a year ago. The crowd was ecstatic. Cheers roared across the South Lawn as you watched, an ear-to-ear smile on your face. Marco Rubio’s watch party resembled a funeral. Of the people who hadn’t already left, people were in shock. The watch party was silent with the only sounds ringing out being people weeping from the shocking loss. As you prepared to give your victory speech, you could only think about one word– historic. Four years ago, you didn’t expect the election to be as close as it was, and now you can finally celebrate your historic win. As you walk out to the stage and the beams shine on you, the roars of the crowd nearly knock you off your feet. This is the moment you have been waiting for your entire career, and you soak in every last second of it.

The energy and excitement of the night stayed with you for the following weeks. Few Republicans had much to say about the night, and when some tried to point to fraud that led to your win, no one left was listening to them. You didn’t expect this to happen; you had hoped your large win would’ve gotten conservatives to hold each other accountable, but no. The infighting on the other side is something you’ve never seen before. Republicans have thrown everything at you, and still lost by a large margin. Not a single person in party leadership knows what else there is to do– the Republican Party, at its core, has changed since your victory. You don’t know what is to come of it, but the party won’t nominate Marco Rubio, or anyone like him, 4 years from now.

Looking forward to the remainder of your presidency, there could be a chance that you could check off some of your unkept promises from the past four years. Your win was able to carry victories to congressional Democrats downballot in races across the country. The House is the closest it’s been in years, and it is now incredibly competitive. As for the Senate, you were able to help Senate Democrats flip several seats to have the Senate be just as competitive as the House. Between your recent victory, conflicts abroad, and a pandemic at home, the stakes for your upcoming legislative priorities could not be higher. Play your cards right, and you could go down in the history books as one of the most consequential presidents of this century thus far.

For now, you have to get to your inauguration first. Getting to January 20th without legitimization pushback should be a breeze given your large win. As for the legislative front, Republicans are dragging their feet on any negotiations, but this could be your window to work out something with them before any talk of the midterms begins. Your first term may not have gone the way you expected it to, but it seems that the country has broken through and believes in the vision you have painted for their future. And, unlike the 1st time, your second term could get you the legacy you had worked for over several decades.
